title: How To Help A Bullied Student
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues against the increasingly common restorative-justice practice of bringing a bullying victim and their bully together for a guided conversation to 'problem solve' and 'repair harm,' calling it a humiliation of the victim that leaves the bully largely unchanged. He explains that bullies won't be talked out of behavior too closely tied to their self-esteem and peer status, and that in a facilitated conversation they'll simply deny, deflect, or grow more cautious and clandestine rather than stop. He lays out what victims actually need — protection, strict accountability applied to the bully, and preserved dignity, without being forced to recount their pain in front of their tormentor — and what bullies need, namely a blunt one-way declaration that bullying is cowardice, not a negotiated conversation. His recommended response is separating the two students entirely and imposing consequences that carry public humility, like watching recess in silence next to the teacher for a week, arguing it's the message and humility that changes behavior, not the specific punishment.
points: Bringing a bullying victim and bully together for a guided 'repair harm' conversation humiliates the victim and rarely changes the bully's behavior.
Bullies won't be talked out of the behavior through dialogue because it's too closely tied to their self-esteem and peer status — expect denial, deflection, or increased secrecy instead.
Victims need protection, visible accountability applied to the bully, and preserved dignity — not to be forced to recount their pain in front of their tormentor.
Tell bullies directly, as a one-way declaration rather than a negotiated conversation, that 'only cowards bully.'

Separate the bully and victim entirely and impose consequences carrying public humility (such as silently watching recess next to the teacher for a week) — the message and humility change behavior, not the specific punishment.
quotes: It’s in vogue these days to bring the victim of bullying and their tormentor together for a guided chitchat.
Bullying, by definition, is an imbalance of power whereby the strong abuses, intimidates, and injures the weak and vulnerable. It’s evil and cowardice.
Those with the propensity to bully will not be dialogued out of it. Trying to do so is a fool’s game.
They need to know that you’ll do everything in your power to protect every student from bullying, not just them.
Bullying is the one of greatest ironies because it confuses insecurity, which has infected the core of the bully, for strength.
Knock the bully’s ego down a peg or ten and send a message to your class by having the bully watch recess for a week, for example, silent and humbled and sitting next to you.
